description: Quantum Horizon is a solo project at the intersection of astrophysics, scientific computing, AI, and interactive data visualization. For NASA Space Apps 2026, I took on Planet X and SPHEREx and built a public blink tool that turns SPHEREx observations into measurements anyone can explore: stars caught moving, asteroids tracked along their orbits, and every number shown with its uncertainty.
summary:
Quantum Horizon is a blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx. Enter a star's name or coordinates, or click any point on its sky map, and it finds every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, aligns them onto one grid and plays them in time order — the method that found Pluto in 1930, applied to an infrared survey that maps the whole sky every six months in 102 bands.

It measures as well as shows. Barnard's Star moves 9.71 ± 1.57 arcseconds in a year against a predicted 10.28, recovered at 6.2σ. The tool builds spectra, follows brightness within narrow wavelength bands, differences any two epochs, overlays Gaia DR3 and searches the field for anything that moved.

It also tracks moving objects. Any of 7,533 asteroids and comets from NASA/JPL can be blinked through every SPHEREx exposure that caught it, each frame centred on JPL's predicted position. Our result: we checked the orbits of the 120 largest main-belt and near-Earth asteroids against SPHEREx, and 116 of the 117 detected sit where JPL predicts, typically within 1.0 arcsecond (0.17 of a pixel). That is the test any search for an unseen planet rests on.

Every number carries an uncertainty and a confidence label, and when the data cannot answer, the tool says so.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Quantum Horizon turns SPHEREx into a tool anyone can use to watch the sky change. Search a name (with suggestions as you type), paste coordinates in degrees or hours, or click any star on the built-in sky map. The tool finds every SPHEREx image covering that position through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, reads only the pixels it needs from the SPHEREx mirror on AWS Open Data, masks unusable pixels, subtracts the modelled zodiacal light, reprojects every frame onto one common grid, and median-stacks each detector within each survey pass. The browser plays one clean frame per pass as a blink, or the difference between any two passes.

LIVE TOOL: https://quantum-horizon-web.vercel.app

ASTEROID RESULT: https://quantum-horizon-web.vercel.app/survey

SLIDES: https://github.com/KhamessiTaha/quantum-horizon/blob/main/docs/quantum-horizon-slides.pdf

A RESULT: JPL'S ORBITS CHECKED AGAINST SPHEREX FOR 120 ASTEROIDS

The Planet X question is about things that move. So the tool also blinks moving objects: IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool lists every SPHEREx exposure that caught an asteroid, JPL Horizons predicts where it should be at each moment, and every frame is cut out around that prediction, so the asteroid holds still while the stars stream past. The measured offset tests the orbit.

We ran this on the 120 largest main-belt and near-Earth asteroids. 117 were detected and measured, and 116 sit where JPL predicts within their uncertainty or one pixel, with a typical offset of 1.0 arcsecond (0.17 of a SPHEREx pixel). The one exception, Fortuna, rests on three frames and is labelled marginal, not claimed as anything. An object only counts as seen if it stands out in the median of all its frames, where the stars cancel; faint objects such as Sedna are reported as not seen rather than matched to a passing star. Any of 7,533 bodies in the Solar System view can be tracked the same way.

EVERY CONSIDERATION IN THE CHALLENGE

• Coordinates in, image series out: RA/Dec in degrees or sexagesimal, played like a little video.

• Easy to update: the archive is queried per position, so new weekly releases appear automatically (QR2, QR3 and DR1 are all supported).

• The 102 bands: each of the six detector arrays is stacked separately for signal-to-noise, and a spectrum is built on the fly for any source you click. A colour view combines three detectors.

• Add and subtract epochs: difference any two passes; drop any pass from the blink and add it back.

• Field of view: 0.03° to 0.2°.

• Overlays: Gaia DR3 stars propagated to each pass date; an interactive sky map on WISE, 2MASS and DSS2 imagery, with named objects you can click to blink.

• URL and embedding: every setting lives in the URL, and any view can be embedded or downloaded as CSV or JSON.

• Metadata: every SPHEREx flag on the source is shown, named and explained.

A MEASUREMENT, NOT AN ANIMATION

Positions are fitted on every frame and on each pass stack, with uncertainties from a leave-one-out jackknife. Motion is reported against the catalog prediction with a significance and a label: measured, marginal, below the noise, or not measurable. Results on the five test targets:

• Barnard's Star: 9.71 ± 1.57″ (D2) and 10.31 ± 1.08″ (D1) against 10.28″ and 10.08″ predicted; two independent detectors agree.

• Epsilon Indi B: 6.57 ± 0.62″ against 6.69″, from 84 exposures over five passes.

• WISE 0855: 11.27 ± 2.97″ against 7.97″, labelled marginal, the honest limit for so faint a source.

• RW Aurigae: no motion (0.36 ± 0.62″), and its brightness rises 121% at 0.74–0.84 µm (12.5σ).

• R Draconis: saturated, and the uncertainty says so.

THREE DECISIONS THE SCIENCE DEPENDS ON

1. Flags: a bright star's own pixels carry saturation and transient flags. Treating them as bad data deleted Barnard's Star in our first run, so flags are split four ways, and only genuinely unusable pixels are masked.

2. Epochs: catalog positions are J2000 (SIMBAD) or J2016 (Gaia); Barnard's Star has moved arcminutes since. Every catalog position is propagated to each frame's date.

3. Wavelength: SPHEREx changes wavelength between exposures of the same pass, so brightness is only compared inside narrow bands.

EXPLORE, THEN BLINK

A 3D map of the 163 stars and brown dwarfs within about 7 parsecs and a 3D Solar System of real orbits lead straight into a blink. Every star and planet model is labelled as an artist's impression from its spectral type, never an image.

HONESTY AS A FEATURE

The tool refuses to report the brightness of a saturated star and explains why, while still measuring its position. Faint asteroids are reported as not seen. Results are labelled measurements or candidates, never discoveries.

BUILT WITH

Python (FastAPI, astropy, reproject, pyvo, s3fs) for the measurement service; React, TypeScript, Vite and three.js for the interface; Aladin Lite for the sky map. Both run on Vercel. NASA's archive was intermittently down during the event, so the tool retries IRSA's services, and the image lists of 189 stars and 128 asteroids ship with it, so they open even when IRSA does not answer. 29 automated tests cover the pipeline, the flag policy, the epoch propagation, the mover search and asteroid tracking. The orbit code for the Solar System view is adapted from my own NASA Space Apps 2024 project, CosmoArchitects.

AI ASSISTANCE

AI tools were used as a coding and writing assistant during development, and to generate the demo video's voice-over (text-to-speech). Every image in the video and slides is a screenshot of the working tool or an output of its code, and every number comes from running this code on real SPHEREx data.

NEXT STEPS

Volunteer review of mover-search candidates, in the spirit of Backyard Worlds and WiseView, and tracking every known asteroid in each blinked field.
